topic: Kerala HC: police cannot hold an arrested person overnight just because it is after 5 PM - guidelines preferring production before magistrates only between 10 AM and 5 PM set aside; Article 22(2) and Section 58 BNSS 24-hour limit is an outer limit, not a right to delay (Adv. P.S. Subeesh v. State of Kerala, WP(PIL) 165/2025, 2026:KER:80664, 2026 LiveLaw (Ker) 599)

slides.title: Arrested after 5 PM? **Liberty does not wait** till morning
slides.subtitle: A government rule cannot push police to keep an arrested person until the next day just because court hours are over.
slides.cite: **Adv. P.S. Subeesh v. State of Kerala**, 2026:KER:80664 · Division Bench

slides.label: The case
slides.title: A **5 PM rule** was challenged
bullets: Kerala government guidelines said arrested persons should, as far as possible, be produced before a magistrate **between 10 AM and 5 PM**.
Production after 5 PM was allowed only in **exceptional circumstances**, with prior intimation to the magistrate.
A public interest petition argued this would **discourage** police from producing people on time.

slides.label: What the court said
slides.title: 24 hours is a **maximum**, not a right
bullets: The 24-hour limit is only the **outer limit**. Police have no general right to wait until it is about to run out.
There is a separate duty to produce the arrested person **without unnecessary delay**.
Waiting till morning can delay **legal help**, a challenge to the arrest, and opposing police custody.
slides.note: **Law fact:** Article 22(2) of the Constitution and Section 58 BNSS say an arrested person must be produced before a magistrate within **24 hours**, not counting travel time.

slides.label: The result
slides.title: The **10-to-5 preference** is gone
bullets: The High Court **set aside** the guidelines to the extent they preferred production between 10 AM and 5 PM.
The rule allowing later production only in "exceptional circumstances" was also **set aside**.
The State must issue **fresh guidelines** in line with the judgment.
slides.note: **Law fact:** An executive protocol **cannot dilute** safeguards given by the Constitution and the law, said the court.

slides.label: Keep in mind
slides.title: What the ruling **does not** say
bullets: The requirement of **prior intimation** to the magistrate for production after 5 PM was **upheld**.
The State can still take **reasonable steps** to protect judicial officers, as long as prompt production is not affected.
This post is for information only, not legal advice.

caption:
An arrest after 5 PM is no excuse to keep someone locked up till the next morning ⏰⚖️

The Kerala High Court has struck down state guidelines that asked police to produce arrested persons before a magistrate, as far as possible, only between 10 AM and 5 PM, and to do so later only in "exceptional circumstances". The court said the 24-hour limit in Article 22(2) of the Constitution and Section 58 of the BNSS is an outer limit. It does not give the police a right to wait until that time is almost over.

The court explained that holding a person overnight just because court hours have ended can delay their access to a lawyer, their chance to challenge the arrest, and their chance to oppose police custody. An executive protocol cannot water down safeguards given by the Constitution and the law.

The court did uphold the requirement of informing the magistrate in advance before producing someone after 5 PM, and said the State may still take reasonable steps for the safety of judicial officers. The State has been directed to issue fresh guidelines in line with the judgment.

Case: Adv. P.S. Subeesh v. State of Kerala & Ors., WP(PIL) 165/2025 | 2026:KER:80664 | 2026 LiveLaw (Ker) 599 | Justice Raja Vijayaraghavan V and Justice K.V. Jayakumar, Kerala High Court | 23 October 2026
